opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to not overreact, but also not dismiss it. In ML especially, you run into this all the time. You have some strong prior, like "this architecture doesn't scale" or "this objective is worse," and then you see one result that contradicts it. The instinct is either to throw everything out or to say "oh, that's just noise, bad baseline, whatever."

What I try to do is ask: how much evidence was my original belief actually built on? A lot of the time, when I'm honest, my "worldview" came from a handful of experiments, maybe at a particular scale, with a particular setup. So if a single clean counterexample shows up, that should move me quite a bit, because the belief wasn't that well-founded to begin with. On the other hand, if the belief comes from many independent results across different settings, then one weird example is more likely to be a special case, and the interesting question becomes *why* it's different.

The other thing is that counterexamples are a gift. They tell you that the world has more structure than your model of it. So rather than asking "is my belief right or wrong," I ask "what's the condition under which both things can be true?" Very often the answer is something like scale, data, or compute regime, and you end up with a more nuanced belief that's way more useful than the original one.

And practically, I think people should hold their beliefs a little more loosely in this field. Things change so fast. Stuff that was "obviously true" two years ago is just wrong now. So I'd rather be someone who updates quickly and occasionally over-updates than someone who's stuck defending a worldview that the field has already moved past.

r001.rationale: It recommends holding beliefs loosely and updating quickly, but does not recommend monitoring whether one's revision rate is too low.

r002.rationale: It treats counterexamples as a reason to examine the conditions behind a belief, but does not suggest questioning other beliefs that may also be wrong.

r003.rationale: It recommends adjusting beliefs based on the strength of the evidence and seeking a more nuanced explanation; it does not say to abandon a worldview when its foundational assumptions are undermined.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most people, myself included, don't update enough. You see one example that contradicts what you believe, and the natural instinct is to explain it away. You say, oh, that's an outlier, that's a weird benchmark, that's a cherry-picked result. And sometimes that's correct! A single data point shouldn't flip your whole worldview. But I think the mistake is treating every counterexample as noise.

The way I try to think about it is, you should ask what kind of belief it is. If it's a belief that was itself built on a lot of evidence, then one example should move you a little, but not a lot. But if you look closely and realize your belief was actually just a vibe, like something you absorbed from Twitter or from what everyone around you was saying, then a single clean counterexample should move you a lot. Because the belief was never really grounded to begin with.

In research this happens all the time. For a long time the field had very strong priors about what architectures could or couldn't do, and then someone shows a result that just shouldn't work under those priors, and people go through this whole process of denial. I've been on both sides of that. I've had beliefs about scaling or about certain architectural choices where I was quite confident, and then the evidence came in and I had to just say, okay, I was wrong about this one.

The thing I'd say is, when you see something that breaks your model, don't immediately try to patch the model. Sit with it for a bit. Try to figure out what the example is actually telling you. Often the example isn't saying your whole worldview is wrong, it's saying one specific assumption inside it is wrong, and if you can find that assumption, that's really valuable. That's where the learning is.

And the other thing is, you have to actually try to reproduce it or understand it deeply. A lot of strong reactions, both over-updating and under-updating, come from people reacting to a headline. If you dig in, it's usually more nuanced than either camp thinks.

r001.rationale: It warns against dismissing counterexamples and recommends calibrating updates, but does not recommend monitoring whether one’s overall rate of belief revision is too low.

r002.rationale: It recommends finding the specific assumption a counterexample challenges, but does not use one mistaken belief as a prompt to question other beliefs.

r003.rationale: It says a single example should not flip an evidence-based worldview and usually recommends locating the specific wrong assumption, rather than abandoning the worldview.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be willing to update, but the size of the update should match the evidence. If you believe something can never happen and you see a convincing example of it happening, then that belief has to change. But one example doesn’t necessarily tell you how common it is, or whether it generalizes.

So I would ask: What exactly did this example disprove? Was my underlying assumption wrong, or was I applying it too broadly? You can preserve the parts of your worldview that still explain things while revising the part that failed. The important thing is to be curious about the contradiction instead of immediately finding a reason to dismiss it.

r001.rationale: It says to size updates to the evidence, but does not recommend monitoring whether one's overall rate of belief revision is too low.

r002.rationale: It recommends examining the assumption a counterexample disproved, but does not suggest using one mistaken belief to question what other beliefs may be wrong.

r003.rationale: It recommends preserving the parts of one's worldview that still explain things and revising only the part that failed, rather than abandoning a worldview with undermined foundations.

sol-6.1.text: I think you have to be willing to say, okay, maybe my mental model is incomplete. One counterexample doesn’t necessarily mean you should throw away everything you believe, but you also shouldn’t explain it away just because it’s inconvenient. Ask which assumption it challenges, how strong the evidence is, and what you would expect to see if you were wrong. Then adjust your confidence accordingly. You can have strong convictions, but you need to leave room for reality to surprise you.

r001.rationale: It recommends adjusting confidence to the evidence, but does not advise monitoring whether one's overall rate of belief revision is too low.

r002.rationale: It asks which assumption a counterexample challenges, but does not use one mistaken belief as a prompt to question other beliefs.

r003.rationale: It says one counterexample need not make you discard everything and recommends adjusting confidence; it does not say foundational challenges can warrant abandoning the worldview.
